Hi ZX,

Some build-side notes on the job types you listed. These are the things that decide whether small fixed-price jobs stay small or turn into weeks of back and forth.

Build each job type once, then deploy it per client
FAQ bots, reminders and quote flows for SMEs are mostly the same build with different data. I’d keep one master workflow per job type and store each client’s details (business name, opening hours, FAQ sheet, handoff contact, WhatsApp phone number ID) in an n8n Data Table or a config sheet. A new client becomes a config row and credentials, not a fresh build. Fixes and improvements go out to every client instead of being patched one copy at a time.

Sort out Meta onboarding before the build starts
Most delays on WhatsApp jobs aren’t the workflow. Business verification, display name approval and number setup can take days, so they belong in your scoping step. Also check early whether the client already runs their business on the WhatsApp Business app with that number. Meta’s coexistence onboarding can let them keep using the app while the Cloud API runs the bot on the same number, but if it isn’t available for their setup, moving the number cuts them off the app. Better to know that before the client signs off.

Booking reminders need approved templates
FAQ replies can be free-form because the customer messaged first, which opens the 24-hour customer service window. Reminders usually go out after that window has closed, so they have to be sent as pre-approved utility templates. Submit the template during scoping, add quick reply buttons (Confirm / Reschedule), and route the button reply back into n8n to update the booking. Meta now bills per template message, so it’s worth telling the client upfront that reminder volume shows up on their Meta bill.

Plan for how Singapore customers actually type
English, Singlish, Mandarin and Malay, often mixed in one message, plus a lot of voice notes. Download the media with the WhatsApp node, transcribe it with the OpenAI node, then run the same FAQ matching on the text. Have the AI reply in the language the customer used, answer only from the FAQ sheet, and send anything outside the sheet to a human with a short summary of the chat so the owner doesn’t have to scroll back.

Quote automation: let the sheet do the maths
Keep the price list in a sheet the owner can edit. The AI step only pulls the job details out of the chat (service, size, location, date). n8n calculates the price from the sheet, never the model. The draft quote then goes to the owner through a “Send and Wait for Response” step for one-tap approval before it reaches the customer. One wrong AI-generated price is enough for an SME to switch the bot off.

PDPA basics
Store only what the job needs, set a retention period for chat logs, and keep reminders transactional. Anything promotional needs opt-in, and STOP should be honoured instantly across every flow for that number, not just the one that received it.

Handover pack
Each job ships with an error workflow that alerts XASIS (not the SME owner) when something fails, a one-page guide on editing the FAQ sheet, and a short test script you can run with the client before handover. That makes your testing step repeatable instead of improvised every time.

Hi ZX,

Some build-side notes on the job types you listed. These are the things that decide whether small fixed-price jobs stay small or turn into weeks of back and forth.

Build each job type once, then deploy it per client
FAQ bots, reminders and quote flows for SMEs are mostly the same build with different data. I’d keep one master workflow per job type and store each client’s details (business name, opening hours, FAQ sheet, handoff contact, WhatsApp phone number ID) in an n8n Data Table or a config sheet. A new client becomes a config row and credentials, not a fresh build. Fixes and improvements go out to every client instead of being patched one copy at a time.

Sort out Meta onboarding before the build starts
Most delays on WhatsApp jobs aren’t the workflow. Business verification, display name approval and number setup can take days, so they belong in your scoping step. Also check early whether the client already runs their business on the WhatsApp Business app with that number. Meta’s coexistence onboarding can let them keep using the app while the Cloud API runs the bot on the same number, but if it isn’t available for their setup, moving the number cuts them off the app. Better to know that before the client signs off.

Booking reminders need approved templates
FAQ replies can be free-form because the customer messaged first, which opens the 24-hour customer service window. Reminders usually go out after that window has closed, so they have to be sent as pre-approved utility templates. Submit the template during scoping, add quick reply buttons (Confirm / Reschedule), and route the button reply back into n8n to update the booking. Meta now bills per template message, so it’s worth telling the client upfront that reminder volume shows up on their Meta bill.

Plan for how Singapore customers actually type
English, Singlish, Mandarin and Malay, often mixed in one message, plus a lot of voice notes. Download the media with the WhatsApp node, transcribe it with the OpenAI node, then run the same FAQ matching on the text. Have the AI reply in the language the customer used, answer only from the FAQ sheet, and send anything outside the sheet to a human with a short summary of the chat so the owner doesn’t have to scroll back.

Quote automation: let the sheet do the maths
Keep the price list in a sheet the owner can edit. The AI step only pulls the job details out of the chat (service, size, location, date). n8n calculates the price from the sheet, never the model. The draft quote then goes to the owner through a “Send and Wait for Response” step for one-tap approval before it reaches the customer. One wrong AI-generated price is enough for an SME to switch the bot off.

PDPA basics
Store only what the job needs, set a retention period for chat logs, and keep reminders transactional. Anything promotional needs opt-in, and STOP should be honoured instantly across every flow for that number, not just the one that received it.

Handover pack
Each job ships with an error workflow that alerts XASIS (not the SME owner) when something fails, a one-page guide on editing the FAQ sheet, and a short test script you can run with the client before handover. That makes your testing step repeatable instead of improvised every time.

Hi ZX. Most replies here offer one builder and one price, so here’s something different: three reasons WhatsApp FAQ bots for SMEs fail after week two, and how to avoid them.

comments.text:
Hi ZX, 
 Some build-side notes on the job types you listed. These are the things that decide whether small fixed-price jobs stay small or turn into weeks of back and forth. 
  Build each job type once, then deploy it per client  
FAQ bots, reminders and quote flows for SMEs are mostly the same build with different data. I’d keep one master workflow per job type and store each client’s details (business name, opening hours, FAQ sheet, handoff contact, WhatsApp phone number ID) in an n8n Data Table or a config sheet. A new client becomes a config row and credentials, not a fresh build. Fixes and improvements go out to every client instead of being patched one copy at a time. 
  Sort out Meta onboarding before the build starts  
Most delays on WhatsApp jobs aren’t the workflow. Business verification, display name approval and number setup can take days, so they belong in your scoping step. Also check early whether the client already runs their business on the WhatsApp Business app with that number. Meta’s coexistence onboarding can let them keep using the app while the Cloud API runs the bot on the same number, but if it isn’t available for their setup, moving the number cuts them off the app. Better to know that before the client signs off. 
  Booking reminders need approved templates  
FAQ replies can be free-form because the customer messaged first, which opens the 24-hour customer service window. Reminders usually go out after that window has closed, so they have to be sent as pre-approved utility templates. Submit the template during scoping, add quick reply buttons (Confirm / Reschedule), and route the button reply back into n8n to update the booking. Meta now bills per template message, so it’s worth telling the client upfront that reminder volume shows up on their Meta bill. 
  Plan for how Singapore customers actually type  
English, Singlish, Mandarin and Malay, often mixed in one message, plus a lot of voice notes. Download the media with the WhatsApp node, transcribe it with the OpenAI node, then run the same FAQ matching on the text. Have the AI reply in the language the customer used, answer only from the FAQ sheet, and send anything outside the sheet to a human with a short summary of the chat so the owner doesn’t have to scroll back. 
  Quote automation: let the sheet do the maths  
Keep the price list in a sheet the owner can edit. The AI step only pulls the job details out of the chat (service, size, location, date). n8n calculates the price from the sheet, never the model. The draft quote then goes to the owner through a “Send and Wait for Response” step for one-tap approval before it reaches the customer. One wrong AI-generated price is enough for an SME to switch the bot off. 
  PDPA basics  
Store only what the job needs, set a retention period for chat logs, and keep reminders transactional. Anything promotional needs opt-in, and STOP should be honoured instantly across every flow for that number, not just the one that received it. 
  Handover pack  
Each job ships with an error workflow that alerts XASIS (not the SME owner) when something fails, a one-page guide on editing the FAQ sheet, and a short test script you can run with the client before handover. That makes your testing step repeatable instead of improvised every time.
